assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED turned a superconducting artificial atom into a controllable, strongly coupled quantum system in a one-dimensional resonator, opening a new regime of microwave quantum optics (dispersive readout, strong coupling, photon-qubit interfaces) and becoming the standard architecture for superconducting quantum processors. It is a clean experiment that makes basic quantum physics visible and controllable, and it is the natural successor to the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits. I know this field closely and rate its originality and lasting impact very highly.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 theory proposal (Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin, Schoelkopf) and the 2004 Nature strong-coupling demonstration (Wallraff et al., Schoelkopf group) are tightly intertwined. Wallraff and Schoelkopf are the experimental pillars and Blais the lead theorist; Girvin is a decisive theory contributor but the three-person cap forces a difficult choice. I also have professional proximity to this community and would flag that.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed across many laboratories over two decades and routinely used in every superconducting-qubit platform (dispersive readout, bosonic codes, hybrid systems). Interpretation is stable and recognition is timely, with the 2025 prize having cleared the prior-recognition question for the underlying circuit physics.
uncertainties: Whether Girvin or Blais should take the theory slot, and whether Schoelkopf and Wallraff fairly share the experimental credit.
Possible overlap or ordering concern with the 2025 laureates' work (Devoret was a close contributor to circuit QED).
My own proximity to this community may bias me toward it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock (magic-wavelength trapping proposed by Katori, then realised to high accuracy and stability by Ye's group) delivers fractional uncertainties around 1e-18 and underpins the coming redefinition of the second, tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy. It is a decisive qualitative advance over single-ion clocks and a clear case of foundational atomic physics enabling a platform.
assessment.attribution: Katori's 2003 magic-wavelength concept and early Sr clock, and Ye's subsequent precision realisations and many-body-clock work, form a natural two-person configuration. Other contributors (Takamoto, Lemonde, Bloom/Ludlow collaborators) exist but the core credit is reasonably clear.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs have confirmed performance at the 1e-18 level and clocks have been compared across continents. Timely; the prize for optical frequency combs in 2005 already recognised part of the metrology chain, so the novelty of this step must be argued clearly.
uncertainties: Overlap with prior metrology prizes (2005 combs, 2012 ion control) and Ye's links to comb work.
Whether Lemonde, Takamoto or Ludlow deserve a share is not resolved by the supplied credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84 and the entanglement-based E91 protocol) is a foundational idea in quantum information in which a basic quantum principle yields a concrete cryptographic primitive. Importance, originality and conceptual clarity are high, and deployments (fibre and satellite links) show real reach.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard (1984) are the clear originators; Ekert (1991) independently introduced the entanglement-based version linked to Bell inequalities. Weiner/Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding ideas are a historical caveat but are not in the credited names. The three-person configuration looks defensible.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations are extensive and the physics is stable, though practical security against side channels remains an engineering issue. The 2022 prize recognised entanglement experiments, so the field is not unrecognised, but the protocol invention itself is mature and timely.
uncertainties: Wiesner's conjugate coding is a priority question not in the credited list.
Practical security and real-world impact are debated, though the discovery is a principle, not a product.
Overlap in theme with the 2022 prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions and Blatt's experimental realisation of its gates and algorithms established ion traps as a leading quantum computing platform with the highest-fidelity gates. This opened a clear new regime of controlled many-body quantum systems and is a natural moment where foundational physics becomes an enabling platform.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the decisive 1995 theory proposal; Blatt's group performed the first Cirac-Zoller gate and many landmark demonstrations. Wineland (Nobel 2012) and others (Monroe, Wineland group gates) are outside the supplied credit, so the allocation between theory and experiment is slightly awkward given prior recognition of ion control.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed across several laboratories and companies, with steady fidelity improvements. Fault-tolerant quantum computing is still ahead, but the physics discovery is mature.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize for ion manipulation (Wineland) reduces novelty.
Competing credit for Monroe and the NIST group, who are not on the credited list.
Cirac and Zoller are also credited in other candidates, so the committee must avoid inconsistent configurations.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics and quantum acoustics showed that macroscopic mechanical objects can be cooled to the ground state and entangled or coherently controlled, including with superconducting qubits (Cleland's phonon-qubit work). This extends quantum control to a new regime of mass and is physically clean and conceptually important, with applications to transduction and sensing.
assessment.attribution: Kippenberg and Aspelmeyer are the leading figures in optical-regime optomechanics, and Cleland in quantum acoustics and the first mechanical quantum ground state (2010). The compound candidate has two sub-fields that may need different recognition, and other key contributors (Teufel, Painter, Schwab, Harris) are not credited.
assessment.maturity: Well reproduced across several labs, but the field is still evolving and the broader consequences (e.g., macroscopic superposition tests) are not yet settled. Recognition is plausible but slightly early.
uncertainties: Credit among Cleland, Teufel, Painter, Schwab and others is unresolved.
Compound candidate that merges optical and acoustic domains.
Applications are still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction and fault-tolerance theory showed that large quantum computations are in principle possible despite decoherence; it is conceptually central to the whole field, and I agree that without full-scale error correction we will not use quantum processors. The theory is deep and original, and recent below-threshold experiments strengthen its relevance.
assessment.attribution: Shor (the first code and fault-tolerance contributions) and Steane (CSS codes) are clear; Kitaev's toric/surface code and anyon-based fault tolerance are also decisive. Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme, Aharonov and Ben-Or, Preskill and others contributed decisively, so the three-person cut is difficult.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations of logical qubits and below-threshold surface codes are recent and still limited, so the practical confirmation is partial. Interpreting a theoretical prize as recognising discovery rather than technology is reasonable, but timing is arguably early.
uncertainties: Many comparably important contributors are excluded by the three-person limit.
Experimental confirmation of scalable fault tolerance is not yet complete.
Whether it is physics rather than computer science is a recurring question.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices provide controllable quantum simulators of Hubbard-type many-body physics, such as the superfluid-Mott transition, single-site resolved quantum gas microscopes and magnetism. It opened a regime of clean, tunable many-body quantum physics.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch, Cirac) provided the theory, Bloch's group the 2002 Mott transition and later developments, and Greiner (with Bloch) the Mott experiment and the quantum gas microscope. Jean Dalibard and Cirac are also credited, and the five-name list is awkward for a three-person prize. Hulet and Esslinger are not credited.
assessment.maturity: Broadly confirmed across many groups; the quantum-simulation payoff is real but the work on difficult regimes such as the fermionic Hubbard model at low temperatures is still unfinished.
uncertainties: The credit boundary between theory and experiment is blurry and the supplied list has five names.
Overlap with the 2001 BEC and 2012 prizes.
Zoller and Cirac recur across candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators and its experimental realisation in HgTe quantum wells opened a major topological direction in condensed matter, linking band structure topology to protected edge states. It is outside my own specialty, so I defer more to colleagues in condensed matter, but its originality and breadth are evident.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical predictions (the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal and Zhang's group also matter and are not credited), and Molenkamp's group made the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect. The configuration is reasonable, but the omission of Zhang and Bernevig is a concern.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in multiple materials and by ARPES in 3D topological insulators, with stable interpretation. Occurring after the 2016 prize for topological phase transitions, so recognition is timely but the novelty relative to that prize must be judged.
uncertainties: Excluded contributors (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore, Hasan) complicate the attribution.
Outside my own expertise, so I defer to the condensed matter colleagues.
Relationship to the 2016 prize.
